en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on False Speech, 10.
The Training Rule on Digging the Earth.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Now at that time, the monks of Āḷavī, while performing construction work, were digging the earth themselves and having it dug by others.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, dig the earth themselves and have it dug by others?"
“The ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, harm living beings with a single sense-faculty.
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [they] grumbled, complained, and criticized:
“How can it be that the monks of Āḷavī dig up the earth themselves and cause it to be dug up?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, monks, that you dig up the earth yourselves and cause it to be dug up?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, dig the earth yourselves or have it dug by others?
For people, foolish men, perceive the earth as a living being.”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘Whatever monk should dig the earth or cause it to be dug, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person...
"a monk" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
As for "earth," there are two kinds of earth: earth that has been formed and earth that has not yet been formed.
What is called "arisen earth" is pure soil, pure clay, with few stones, few pebbles, few gravel, few sand, and few grit; it is mostly soil, mostly clay.
Even when not burnt, it is called "arisen earth."
Even a heap of dust or a heap of clay that has been left for more than four months is called "earth that has arisen.
Earth that is "unarisen" refers to pure rock,
pure gravel, pure potsherds, pure pebbles, or pure sand, containing little dust.
[The earth] consists mostly of stones, mostly gravel, mostly potsherds, mostly sand, and mostly dust.
Even when burnt, it is called "unborn earth.
Furthermore, even a heap of dust or a heap of clay that has been left for less than four months is also called "unborn earth."
"Should dig" means she digs herself; there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Should cause to dig" means...
If he commands another, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having been commanded once, he digs even many times, there is an offense of expiation.
If, perceiving earth as earth, he digs or causes it to be dug, breaks it or causes it to be broken, or burns it or causes it to be burned, there is an offense of expiation.
If one digs, or causes to be dug, breaks, or causes to be broken, burns, or causes to be burned, while being doubtful that it is earth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one digs, or causes to be dug, breaks, or causes to be broken, burns, or causes to be burned, perceiving what is not earth as earth, there is no offense.
If one perceives earth as not earth, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not earth and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not earth and he perceives it as not earth, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If one says, "Know this," "Give this," "Bring this," "There is need for this," or "Make this allowable," unintentionally and through lack of mindfulness, [it is an offense of wrong-doing].
For one who does not know,
for one who is insane,
and for an original offender.
The tenth training rule concerning digging the earth is finished.
This is the first section, on false speech.
Its summary verse:
Musā, omasapesuññaṃ,
and two for lying on a couch;
except when [spoken] by one who knows, and [when it is] true.
A grave offense is an immediate offense.
